strong_form: Progress against cancer mortality has been slow mainly because the main cellular defenses against cancer (p53/RB-driven senescence and apoptosis, telomere limits) promote aging, and the main anti-aging changes promote cancer; therefore interventions that strengthen anti-cancer defenses should reliably accelerate aging, and vice versa.
weak_form: Cellular senescence is antagonistically pleiotropic: it suppresses tumors early but contributes to aging and late-life cancer, which constrains some anti-cancer and anti-aging strategies.
refuted_if: Animals with strengthened tumor suppressors that are cancer-resistant yet age normally or longer (observed: super-p53 and super-p53/Arf mice); or large sustained declines in cancer mortality achieved without such tradeoffs (observed: ~33% US decline since 1991 from tobacco control, screening, treatment).

prior_art.citation: Campisi, 'Senescent Cells, Tumor Suppression, and Organismal Aging: Good Citizens, Bad Neighbors' (Cell 2005)
Berkeley Lab news, 'Cellular senescence: a double-edged sword' (2008), Campisi on tradeoffs between early fitness and late-life survival
Buck Institute, 'Escape cancer, but age sooner'
Garcia-Cao et al. 2002 EMBO J, super p53 mice cancer-protected with no premature aging
Nature news 2007 on Matheu et al.: super p53/Arf mice resist cancer and live longer on average
Fierce Healthcare: US cancer death rate down 33% since 1991

strongest_criticism: The tradeoff is real at the level of senescence biology but not a hard constraint: regulated boosts to p53/Arf gave cancer resistance with normal or longer lifespan, so 'defenses against one feed the other' is not a law. And the war on cancer did not simply stall; mortality has fallen about a third since 1991 for reasons (smoking, screening, treatment) unrelated to the tradeoff, so the explanation of the stall is at best partial.
